Step 1 showed one 401. Here are five, and why the caller matters. Every agent gets a passport. SPIFFE is the naming standard. SPIRE hands each agent a signed token, an SVID. Think of a sealed envelope with a passport inside, addressed to one recipient.

Look at the left. Five bad credentials, sent straight to the gateway, no model involved. All five got HTTP 401. The red row is a genuine SPIRE token, real signer, real name. It was only addressed to payments-mcp instead of the gateway. Refused.

Now the right. The caller is half the lookup key. Same rule: settlement-agent may pay up to its limit, the reviewer-ui may pay only a payment that is waiting for a human, and anyone else gets no row. "Identity is an input to the decision, not a label on it."

IF THERE IS TIME, run it live. No model call, no browser, costs nothing. From the repo root:
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/e2e/test_policy_denial.py -v -k "criterion_4 or criterion_5"
SAY: "Criterion 4 is a walk over the source proving there is no policy logic in the settlement agent or the MCP server at all. Criterion 5 speaks MCP to the gateway directly with two different SPIRE-minted identities, and shows the verdict change with the caller."
Running it adds time; budget about a minute.

KASPER

Optional. Ring 1 · Reach has two layers, and William's demo shows one of them: Linkerd.

Plain words first. In his OSFF demo William used Linkerd, a service mesh: a small proxy beside every pod that checks the caller's identity at the destination's door. Our demo runs it too, for the way in. For the way out we use plain Kubernetes network policy, enforced in the node. The two do different jobs, and the choice came from a spike on 2026-10-12, on a separate cluster.

Left, Linkerd. Every attempt to go around the gateway, to payments-mcp or to the decision service, is refused with HTTP 403: a refusal you can read, where our old network layer gave silence. And the proxy counts every refusal, per policy. That held in the spike for pods with no proxy at all, and for pods told to skip it.

Right, network policy. The agents may reach the gateway, and no address on the internet: not even the model provider, because the model sits behind the gateway too, and only the gateway reaches it. Linkerd's own egress rule couldn't do this job: it applies to a whole namespace, it matches only the server name the client claims, the SNI, and a pod that skips its proxy skips the rule. Network policy is enforced in the node, whether the pod cooperates or not.

SAY: "So reach has two layers: identity at the destination, and addresses in the node. Linkerd does the first; network policy does the second."

SAY, plainly, what we gave up: "Between meshed pods, egress is decided per pod, not per port: a pod allowed to reach a peer's proxy (4143) can reach any port on that peer that listens on the pod IP; which ports answer is decided by the peer's Linkerd Servers, per port and per identity. And an egress drop is still silent: nothing answers and nothing counts it. Linkerd's refusals are loud: counted, and the proxy adds a span when the request carries a trace header."

SAY, before someone in the room does: "One caveat for a regulated audience: open-source Linkerd ships edge releases only. Its last open-source stable release was February 2024; stable builds now come from vendors."

IF ASKED about the trace: proxy tracing is on. The claim stays one trace, and the proxies add spans, four for each meshed hop: in the spike, 149 spans became 293. They are named by request path and carry no policy data. They put the mesh in the waterfall, nothing more. The control plane's own tracing stays off.

[verify: Linkerd edge-26.10.1 is the pinned release; the live run on Linkerd is still pending when this was written, so say "designed and measured in a spike", not "measured on this cluster"]

Source: Linkerd spike report, 2026-10-12 (criteria 1, 3, 4 and 6; the trace result; release channels); bounded-ai/README.md (Ring 1 · Reach)

KASPER

Why does an agent need all this more than a normal service? In a normal system you can draw the call graph, the map of who calls whom, on a whiteboard before it runs.

An agent is different. On the left, one prompt: "settle this car-damage claim". Then the same prompt, run three times. Run one reads the claim, then pays. Run two reads the claim, and stops to ask a human. Run three checks the policy instead of the claim, and pays. And the pink bars are the tokens each run used, so even the cost changes.

Like a taxi driver who picks a new route every ride. The code tells you what the agent may do, not what it will do. The model draws the call graph at run time. A test that passed on run two tells you nothing about run three.

So if you can't draw the path in advance, you record it as it happens. Here's what got recorded for the Large claim.

Source: Ch 1 (Figure 1.x, relabelled 2026-10-20 from a free-plan-accounts example to a claim settlement, so it rhymes with the demo)

KASPER

Here's what got recorded. Nobody wrote an audit log. Here's the Large claim from the demo, start to finish.

The customer wrote their claim, and the claims agent's model call recorded exactly what it was given. The model read eighty-five hundred euros, and the same span recorded what it answered. The policy service decided: deny, limit six thousand, in its own span. A person approved it, four seconds later, and the reviewer UI recorded who. And the ledger paid, recorded by the payment service.

Five services, five records, joined by the claim id and by trace links. And every one of them speaks the same open standard: OpenTelemetry. So let's look at that from a thousand miles up.

SAY: "Nobody wrote an audit log. The system recorded what it did."

Source: demo evidence for CLM-INTAKE-E59B79 (2026-10-27): reviewer kasper.nissen after 4 s, PAY-000018; Jaeger traces 1a7c8e68… (submit) and 0567a212… (approval)

KASPER

Everything in that evidence is OpenTelemetry, so first the 1,000-mile view.

Two words. A span is the record of one step, like one tool call. A trace is every span of one run, held together by one trace id that every hop passes on, through MCP and A2A too. Drop it at one hop and the story falls apart.

On the left, where telemetry is born. Instrumentation: the OpenTelemetry API and SDK in our own code, auto-instrumentation for the frameworks we didn't write. And the infrastructure: Kubernetes, and here the Linkerd proxies, which emit spans of their own.

All of it goes to one place: the OpenTelemetry Collector. It receives traces, metrics and logs, processes them, and exports them to whatever backend you choose. Here that is Jaeger for traces, Prometheus for metrics, and Dash0 for all three. Analysis tools sit on top of the backends.

The point: you instrument once, in an open standard, and the backend is a choice you can change later.

SAY: "Generate once, send anywhere. The backend is a choice, not a rewrite."

Keep five words: span, one step. Trace, one run. Propagation, the id passed hop to hop. Link, two traces joined. Names, what each attribute means. Each of the next slides is one of them.

The claim crossed two protocols on its way. Here they are.

Source: deploy/observability/collector-config.yaml (receivers, processors, exporters to Jaeger, Prometheus and Dash0)

KASPER

Two protocols carried every hop you just saw.

On the left, MCP, the Model Context Protocol. It reaches down, from an agent to a tool. The agent asks the tool server: what can you do? tools/list. The server answers with its tools. The model picks one and calls it, here execute_payment with an amount, and gets a result back. Call, answer. That's it.

On the right, A2A, Agent2Agent. It reaches across, from one agent to another. First the claims agent reads the other agent's card: who are you, what can you do, where do I find you. Then it hands over a task: settle this claim. And the task lives: working, then input required, waiting on someone, then completed. When it's done, the settlement agent pushes the result back.

The platform questions differ. For MCP: which tool, which arguments, who is asking? For A2A: who may delegate to whom, and does the original identity survive the hand-off?

Both are open, both sit in the Agentic AI Foundation. And notice what neither of them does: decide what an agent is allowed to do. That's the platform's job, which William just showed you.

[verify: MCP and A2A both in AAIF (A2A joined 2026-08-17) — week of]
[verify: A2A task states include working, input-required, completed]

Neither protocol carries the trace for you. So how did one trace id get across all of it?

Source: Ch 2; agents/claims-agent/delegation.py; tools/payments-mcp/server.py

KASPER

One trace id, carried across every hop. Read it top to bottom; it's the claim's path.

The browser starts the trace and sends traceparent as an HTTP header, and the claim id rides along as baggage.

Claims agent to settlement agent is A2A. The traceparent is in the header, but the a2a SDK doesn't read it, so we do, ourselves. That's an upstream gap we filed.

Settlement agent to the gateway is MCP. The id goes in the message itself, params dot underscore meta, the convention MCP adopted, and in the header too.

The gateway asks the policy service over a gRPC hook, and forwards the traceparent, so the policy decision lands in the same trace.

Then on to the tool and the ledger: MCP, then plain HTTP.

The one hop that can't be one trace is the person. Someone approves minutes later, so that's a new trace, with a span link back to the agent's. That's the next slide but one.

And underneath all of it, Linkerd's proxies add their own spans to the same trace, on every meshed hop.

SAY: "Drop the id at one hop, and the story falls apart."

Source: docs/telemetry-contract.md (customer-ui row and CORS allow_headers; a2a-sdk Gap 1 and main.py StarletteInstrumentor workaround; MCP trace context via params._meta, SEP-414; policy-decision-service row: agentgateway forwards traceparent to the guardrail hook; reviewer-ui span links; Linkerd proxy spans)

KASPER

This is the Large claim's trace, the one I opened from the evidence, drawn without the plumbing. One trace from the browser to the decision. Read it like the line under it says: indented means called by the line above, struck through means it never happened.

1. The root, northstar.claim.submit, in the customer's browser, carries the claim id. Every span after it carries it too.
2. The claims agent's chat span: with content capture on, it holds what the customer wrote and what the model read. That's the GenAI semantic conventions: gen_ai.input.messages, gen_ai.output.messages, the system instructions, the model, the tokens.
3. The settlement agent proposes, permitted, then asks for execute_payment. The gateway's tools/call carries jwt.sub, the caller's SPIFFE ID.
4. northstar.policy.decision: deny, eighty-five hundred over the agent's limit of six thousand at autonomous. A refusal is the platform working, so it is not an ERROR on the decision span. The Guardrail span's gRPC status zero says the call to the decision service worked: "the policy said no" stays different from "the policy service was down".
5. The struck-through lines: the gateway's call to payments-mcp, the tool's execute_payment, and the ledger's execute. Never attempted.
SAY: "The execute never reached the tool. The absence is the evidence." That only holds because we never sample.

Not shown: Linkerd's proxies add their own spans, one per side of every meshed hop: 148 of this trace's 304 spans are linkerd-proxy.

Source: Jaeger trace 703c00f1880d8973b696a2c257ccf1be, measured 2026-10-27; Ch 5 (Figure 5.5), Ch 6 (Figure 6.13); docs/telemetry-contract.md "Linkerd proxy spans"

KASPER

Maker and checker. The agent makes the payment. A human checks it. These are two traces, and the slide shows both.

1. Left, trace A: the maker. The agent proposes: the claim came in, the agent asked to execute the payment, and the platform said a person decides. The agent records "input required" and its work is done: trace A ends at the hand-off. Nothing polls while the claim waits, and nothing moved.
2. Right, trace B: the checker. A person approves it. The reviewer-ui records northstar.review.decision, asks the gateway to execute the payment under its own identity and its own rule, human-approved.execute, and then resumes the claim. The decision service has read the ledger and seen that the payment is waiting for a human, so it permits. When the claim completes, the platform pushes the outcome to the customer's page.
SAY: "Nothing was overridden. A different caller was asked about."
The empty middle is the point: human time. Minutes, maybe hours, and nothing runs or polls while the claim waits.
3. The dashed line is a span link: B's resume points back to A. A link, not a parent. "Work separated by human time is two traces and a link. Nothing polls while the claim waits." A parent edge would have misstated both the duration and what was executing.
4. The bottom line is a Prometheus question: how long do humans take? One histogram, by autonomy level and decision. The 95th percentile per level shows whether widening the band really cut the human's load.

Honest limits: Reject is final and the customer is told their claim was declined; but there is no second approver, no timeout, no expiry, and no login on the reviewer-ui. The reviewer id is a string the form supplies.

Every span you've seen has names on it. Who says the names are right?

Source: docs/demo-runbook.md (step 2, the Large claim); docs/telemetry-contract.md (trace B, northstar_approval_wait_duration_seconds); Ch 8

KASPER

Every name in the demo's trace comes from somewhere. The semantic conventions name the common things: http-dot-something for web calls, gen_ai-dot-something for model and agent calls.

But a policy decision, a human review, an autonomy level: those names are ours, and no convention covers them. So we write them down in Weaver, OpenTelemetry's own tool for this. Define them in YAML, on top of the official conventions. Check the registry in CI. Generate the docs from it. And live-check: the Collector sends Weaver a copy of everything the cluster really emits, and it fails if we emit a name we never defined.

Telemetry names are an API. Weaver checks the API against what really runs.

So the record is complete, and its names are checked. Last word: Prove. Who grades the agent?

Source: telemetry/registry (manifest.yaml: northstar on semantic-conventions v1.44.0; policy.yaml northstar.policy.decision); scripts/check-registry.sh (otel/weaver v0.28.0: registry check, registry generate markdown); deploy/observability/weaver-live-check.yaml and telemetry/live-check.toml (fail_on = violation)

Now we read what the bouncer writes down, for one permitted payment. Follow the rows down. First: tools/call, the request as it arrived. Twenty-two keys. jwt.sub is who asked, and gen_ai.tool.name is the only place the tool is named. Second: Guardrail, nine keys: the gateway phoning the policy service. grpc.status zero means the call worked, not what the answer was. Third: the policy service's span holds the why: rule, limit, amount. Fourth: the outbound call, six keys, and no jwt.sub, because the token was stripped. At the bottom: the four keys a refusal adds to span one. On a deny, span four doesn't exist.

The gateway marks its span ERROR with reason MCP, but the refusal travels inside a successful HTTP response: a tool result marked isError, with the rule, the limit and the amount in its text, ending in a short tag the agent reads. Before the detail, one idea: defence in depth. Think of airport security. You walk down a corridor, show your passport, go through the scanner, and meet the gate staff. No single check is trusted to catch everything. Each one assumes the one before it failed.

Next: the eight checks between an agent and a payment.

Source: Ch 7

KASPER

This is the question every platform team asks in an agent review: how do we limit what an agent can do with an MCP server? Here is Northstar's airport.

Read it from the top down. That is the order one tool call travels. Each row has three parts. On the left, the layer. In the middle, what it stops. On the right, what you would show an auditor as proof.

Rows two to four: who is calling, is the token real, is this call allowed. Row five: if the checker is down, the answer is no. Row eight: a human can overturn a refusal, but only by asking again as a different caller.

The one to remember is row one. Seven layers leave a span. The network doesn't. Its proof is BPF maps and TCP probes. A trace records what happened. Only network policy shows what couldn't happen.

Source: Ch 7

KASPER

There are two ways for the platform to say no. The gateway can do it alone, with one line of config: no payment over fifty thousand, for anyone. It answers 403 and says nothing else. The decision service is a service we wrote: it has the live dial, the rule's name, a reason the model can explain, and its own span. We use both. The gateway holds the hard ceiling; the service makes the decision.

Read the table top to bottom. Code to write: none against a service. Sees the tool's arguments: both, since agentgateway 1.6. Changes live: the gateway reloads its config in about a third of a second; the service reads a flag and nothing reloads. Says why: the gateway says "authorization failed" and nothing else; the service names the rule and the limit. In the trace: the gateway leaves one span; the service leaves northstar.policy.decision.

The line at the bottom is the real rule, from the config file. It is an allow rule on purpose: a deny rule lets a string amount through, and we measured that. The ceiling is not in the live demo. scripts/demo ceiling shows it if someone asks.

[verify: agentgateway is a Linux Foundation project hosted in AAIF, not CNCF.]

Source: docs/architecture.md "Two ways to say no"; tests/e2e/test_gateway_ceiling.py

KASPER

The gateway has a second family of guardrails, for the model's own traffic. We read the list from the source, at the v1.6.0 tag. Regex rules mask or reject text. Personal data, like card numbers and emails, is found and masked. A moderation model can judge a prompt. A webhook lets your own service judge. And there are connectors for Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, Azure Content Safety and Google Model Armor.

SAY, plainly: "Northstar's model calls go through the gateway. None of these guards are switched on." The gateway checks who is calling and which model; it does not read the prompt.

Source: agentgateway v1.6.0, crates/agentgateway/src/llm/policy/ (mod.rs, pii/, webhook.rs, moderation.rs, bedrock_guardrails.rs, azure_content_safety.rs, google_model_armor.rs)

KASPER

There are two ways for a platform to say no. William's demo shows one, Northstar shows the other. They're layers, not rivals.

On the left: hide. In William's OSFF demo the gateway has a static allowlist, one CEL line: the tool's name must be in this list. Anything else isn't there. Ask the gateway for its list of tools, and the forbidden one never appears. Call it anyway, and you get HTTP 400, Unknown tool. Think of a building where the vault isn't on the map. The agent can't even ask for it.

On the right: refuse and record. Our payment tool isn't hidden. You saw it in step 1: with the settlement agent's identity, tools/list shows all four tools, execute_payment included. Listed is not permitted: every call is decided. It can't be hidden, because paying claims is the agent's job. Whether a call is fine depends on its arguments: at autonomous the limit is six thousand: five thousand eight hundred, yes. Six thousand two hundred, no. At assisted the limit is zero, so even five thousand eight hundred waits for a person. So the call is proposed, refused, recorded as a northstar.policy.decision span with the rule and the limit, and explained, to the customer now and to an auditor later.

Use both. Hide what an agent must never touch. Refuse, and record, the rest. And credit where it's due: the hide layer, and the rings you've been seeing all along, are William's.

"The platform API is the resource. kubectl and Backstage are just views a person uses to read and change it." And as step 4 showed, who may write it is enforced too. managedFields records who wrote a value last, but the next write wipes it, like a whiteboard. That's why Backstage writes one span per flip, which survives the revert and the pod. The CLI flip in step 3 writes none; the evidence for it is the claim's own northstar.policy.decision, which names the level it was decided under.
